hints: Think what any electrode potential must be measured against, since a single half cell voltage cannot be measured on its own.
Recall the three standard values for concentration, temperature and gas pressure that make the comparison fair.
walkthrough:
Picture why a reference is needed**
You can never dip a voltmeter into one beaker and read an absolute potential. You always need two half cells to make a circuit. By agreement, chemists chose hydrogen as the zero reference, so every other half cell is connected to it and the voltage you read is its standard electrode potential.

Lock in the standard conditions**
For the number to be called standard, everything that affects electrode position must be fixed. That means all dissolved ions at $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, temperature at $298\text{ K}$ ($25^{\circ}\text{C}$) and any gas at $1\text{ atm}$ pressure. The standard hydrogen electrode itself is $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$ at $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$, $\text{H}_{2}(\text{g})$ at $1\text{ atm}$, Pt electrode at $298\text{ K}$.

Final answer: The e.m.f. / voltage of a half-cell compared with / measured against a standard hydrogen electrode.
Under standard conditions of $1\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ for ions, $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ for gases.

hints: Decide which half cell can use the metal itself as the electrode and which one needs an inert platinum electrode because both species are in solution.
Remember the two external items needed to complete the circuit and measure the voltage while keeping the two solutions separate but ionically connected.
List exactly which ions must be present in each beaker to establish the $\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}$ and $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ equilibria.
walkthrough:
Choose the correct electrode material**
Sit beside the two half cells. $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}$ includes a solid metal, so a clean Mg wire can act as the electrode directly. $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 5\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ has no solid metal, both manganese species are in solution, so you must provide an inert surface for electron transfer. That is Pt wire, it conducts but takes no part in the reaction.

Add the solutions**
The Mg beaker needs $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq})$, typically $\text{MgSO}_{4}$ or $\text{Mg(NO}_{3})_{2}$. The Pt beaker needs all the species in the ionic equation together: $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and excess $\text{H}^{+}$ for the acidic conditions.

Complete the circuit correctly**
Join the two solutions with a salt bridge, usually filter paper soaked in $\text{KNO}_{3}(\text{aq})$, to allow ion flow without mixing. Join the two metals with wire through a high resistance voltmeter so almost no current is drawn and the cell stays under standard conditions.

Final answer: Left beaker: Mg wire dipping into solution containing $\text{Mg}^{2+}(\text{aq})$.
Right beaker: Pt wire dipping into solution containing $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}(\text{aq})$, $\text{Mn}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ and $\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$.
The two beakers linked by a salt bridge, electrodes joined by external wires through a voltmeter to give a complete circuit.

hints: Compare the $E^{\ominus}$ values in Table 3.1 to decide which half cell oxidises and releases electrons into the external wire.
walkthrough:
Let the $E^{\ominus}$ values tell you the roles**
$\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}$ is $-2.38\text{ V}$, very negative, so Mg is a powerful reducing agent and readily gives away electrons: $\text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-}$. $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is $+1.52\text{ V}$, very positive, so it readily accepts electrons. Electrons therefore push out of the Mg electrode, making it the negative pole, and are consumed at the Pt electrode, making it the positive pole. Mark $-$ on Mg, $+$ on Pt and draw the $\text{e}^{-}$ arrow from Mg to Pt.

Final answer: Mg electrode is negative ($-$), Pt / $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ electrode is positive ($+$). Electrons $\text{e}^{-}$ flow in external wire from Mg to Pt, arrow pointing towards the $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ half-cell.

hints: Pick the two $E^{\ominus}$ values from Table 3.1 and use $E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{positive} - E^{\ominus}_{negative}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract carefully**
Think of $E^{\ominus}_{cell}$ as the driving force gap between the electron acceptor and the electron donor:
$$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = E^{\ominus}_{cathode} - E^{\ominus}_{anode}$$
Here cathode is $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ at $+1.52\text{ V}$, anode is $\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}$ at $-2.38\text{ V}$. So $$E^{\ominus}_{cell} = 1.52 - (-2.38) = 3.90\text{ V}$$ Keep the plus sign logic clear, subtracting a negative adds on.

hints: Write the two half equations in the reacting direction, Mg oxidised and $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ reduced, then balance the electrons exchanged.
walkthrough:
Scale to cancel electrons**
Write what really happens. Oxidation: $\text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-}$. Reduction: $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 8\text{H}^{+} + 5\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 4\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. The first moves 2 electrons, the second needs 5 electrons. The lowest common multiple is 10, so multiply Mg by 5 and $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ by 2. Adding gives:
$$5\text{Mg} + 2\text{MnO}_{4}^{-} + 16\text{H}^{+} \rightarrow 5\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 8\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$
Check atoms and charge: $+14$ on each side, balanced.

hints: Apply Le Chatelier to $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}$ when $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]$ is lowered by dilution.
walkthrough:
See dilution as shifting the Mg equilibrium**
Focus on $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}$. Adding water lowers $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]$. To oppose this, the equilibrium moves left to make more $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, releasing electrons more readily. That makes the Mg half cell even more negative and an even stronger reducing agent. The gap to the $+1.52\text{ V}$ half cell therefore gets larger, so the cell reaction is even more spontaneous in the same direction. There is no reversal, no change in the equation, just a larger driving force.

Final answer: No change in direction of cell reaction, reaction still proceeds as in (v). Dilution lowers $[\text{Mg}^{2+}]$ so $\text{Mg}^{2+}/\text{Mg}$ equilibrium shifts left, electrode potential becomes even more negative, $E_{cell}$ increases.

hints: Start from the cathode equation $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mg}$ to find how many electrons, and therefore how much charge, are needed for one Mg atom.
Link total charge to current with $Q = It$, remembering to convert 15.0 minutes into seconds.
walkthrough:
Count the total charge to make the Mg atoms**
Each Mg atom needs 2 electrons: $\text{Mg}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Mg}$. Charge on one electron is $1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. So total charge is number of atoms times electrons per atom times charge per electron:
$$Q = 4.75 \times 10^{22} \times 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$$
$$Q = 15200\text{ C}$$
Alternatively with moles: $n(\text{Mg}) = 4.75 \times 10^{22} / 6.02 \times 10^{23}$, then $Q = n \times 2 \times 96500 \approx 15230\text{ C}$.

Convert time and apply $Q = It$**
Current is charge per second, so time must be in seconds: $t = 15.0 \times 60 = 900\text{ s}$. Then:
$$I = Q/t = 15200/900 = 16.9\text{ A}$$
That is the constant current needed, to 3 significant figures with unit A.

Final answer: Total charge $Q = 4.75 \times 10^{22} \times 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19} = 15200\text{ C}$
Current $I = Q/t = 15200/(15.0 \times 60) = 16.9\text{ A}$
